newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.

text.p: RURAL TRAINEESHIPS ANNOUNCED
The Federal Government has announced a new rural traineeship scheme designed to cater for the 30 per cent of young people who leave school before year 12 and don't intend going on to further study.
The government's providing 1-point-four-million dollars to create one-thousand new jobs in the cattle, sheep and wool, grains, poultry, and chemical-use industries.
Federal Training Minister David Kemp says the traineeships will be designed by rural industry bodies, and should be available from March next year.
Mr Kemp has rejected suggestions the rural sector is too depressed to take a-thousand new jobs.
He says injecting traineeships into industries suffering downturns in demand, will help ensure their long term survival.
SECOND MAN CHARGED OVER BONDI FATAL BASHING
A second man has been charged over the killing of a British tourist at Bondi 11 days ago.
A 23 year old Bondi man has been charged with being an accessory after the fact, and will appear in Waverley Local Court later this afternoon.
22 year old Aaron Martin appeared in court yesterday charged with the murder of Brian Hagland.
Police allege Mr Hagland was bashed to death near a popular cafe in the early hours of Saturday, September the 7th.
The second man has been charged after being interviewed by police twice - he voluntarily provided police with a blood sample yesterday.
POLITICAL HAGGLING OVER APPOINTS TO SYDNEY OLYMPICS BOARD
The New South Wales Opposition is to accept a seat on the board of SOCOG, the committee organising the Sydney Olympics.

But the coalition is insisting the seat won't be at the expense of board members like former State Premier Nick Greiner. The coalition has foreshadowed attempts to change the SOCOG Act in the Upper House.
Opposition leader Peter Collins says Olympics minister Michael Knight is planning a political pay-back by not re-appointing Mr Greiner to the board when his term expires on New Year's Eve.
COMPLAINTS TO OMBUDSMAN RISE 28 PERCENT
There's been a 28 percent rise in the number of complaints make to the Commonwealth Ombudsman in the last financial year.
But, despite the increasing workload for the office, Ombudsman, Philippa Smith says proposed funding cuts could mean that in the future, people with complaints are turned away.
Last financial year the office dealt with a record 22-thousand complaints.
But Ms Smith says the cuts to staff and resources will compromise the office's ability to perform it's function.
Most of the complaints made to the ombudsman were about the department of social security, the child support agency and the tax office.
INTERNATIONAL VISITORS ARE HAPPY CAMPERS
A survey of international visitors to Australia last year has found that almost all of those surveyed were happy with the cost and quality of accommodation during their stay.
But it also found that many visitors weren't satisfied with shopping hours, and the lack of foreign language signs.
The Bureau of Tourism Research survey shows Australia received 3-point-7 million overseas visitors in 1995.
That's an 11 percent increase on the previous year.
Korea provided the biggest jump in arrivals, with 57-thousand more visitors last year, than in 1994.
